transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-02-14
Start time: 21:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Evan Park (CTO, Crowne Capital), Lina Patel (Product Manager), Samir Rao (Lead Infra)

Summary: quick discovery focused on per-token cost sensitivity, tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private, caching/batching levers, and compliance constraints for retail-financial workloads. Customer wants a primer and an initial benchmark to validate numbers for an internal ROI doc.

Topics: budget thresholds, latency targets, batch sizing, KV cache impacts, residency & K M S questions, pilot scope and timeline.

--- Transcript ---
00:00 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, happy valentine's day for those celebrating, um we're Maya from Redwood, as a quick intro we do inference hosting across hosted, dedicated and private deployments and today we'd love to understand your budget constraints and what success looks like.
00:12 Evan: yeah thanks Maya, I'm Evan, CTO at Crowne. We have Lina and Samir with us. We're investigating options to power a conversational assistant in our trading operations, so cost per invocation is a huge focus. We'll be blunt: burn rate matters.
00:24 Lina: yes and the product team wants less than 200ms median latency for short prompts, which sounds tight but it's for quick lookups. Also we have to retain audit logs for seven years — compliance is non-negotiable.
00:37 Samir: infrastructure side, we run mostly in a VPC on Oracle Cloud and also have some GCP for analytics. We need to know if Redwood Private is feasible or if Dedicated with VPC peering will hit our residency and K M S requirements.
00:52 Diego: great, thanks. Quick clarifying question — when you say cost per invocation, do you have a rough token or prompt size? And what's the concurrency pattern?
00:58 Evan: initial phase ~3k active users in alpha, average prompt plus completion ~220 tokens, but a lot of short 30-50 token requests too. Peak concurrency around 120-150 QPS but bursty. Our budget is... we were hoping to keep net inference spend under $40k/month in pilot if possible.
01:15 Maya: ok that helps. So two levers we'll talk about today: model/quantization selection and batching/caching. Also routing — hosted fallbacks vs dedicated capacity — can reduce cost if you permit some variability.
01:29 Lina: can you explain caching? we've heard of KV cache but not sure how it helps for short prompts.
01:34 Diego: sure. So KV cache is the key/value cache for decoder states; for repeated conversational prefixes or system prompts we can avoid recomputing early tokens. For short, non-repeating prompts you get less benefit, but for chat with stable system prompt and some reuse, it can cut token compute by 15-40% depending on hit rate. Sometimes transcribers write 'KV cash' in notes, that's a common autocorrect.
01:55 Samir: what's the difference between batching and padding then? Because if we batch too aggressively do we blow up latency?
02:01 Diego: exactly. Batching groups requests to use GPU throughput more efficiently — you're paying per microsecond of kernel time but amortizing GPU overhead across tokens. Padding is when shorter sequences are padded up to the longest in the batch, which increases compute. So optimal batching profiles vary by model size and prompt lengths. Redwood's runtime can do continuous batching to keep tail latency bounded, but there's a latency/cost knob.
02:25 Evan: the numbers we got in-house for a 7B dense model looked like $0.0008 per token — that feels high for our volume. What's typical on Hosted?
02:34 Maya: hosted rates vary by model family; ballpark for common open 7B variants we see effective per-token costs in the $0.00025–$0.0006 range when you use batching + caching. Dedicated nets different economics — reserved GPU pools can reduce unit costs further if you commit, but you take on base capacity spend.
02:52 Lina: can you give an example tradeoff? like if we hit a $40k/month budget what's the realistic throughput with those costs?
02:58 Diego: quick mental math: assume avg 220 tokens per session, at $0.0004/token that's about $0.088 per session. With $40k/month that's ~455k sessions/mo or about 15k/day. That maps to concurrency questions. If you reduce tokens via prompt engineering and caching you can lower that to $0.06 per session.
03:18 Evan: prompt engineering is on our roadmap but not ready for alpha. We need platform levers now. Also we could consider quantized models — what's the hit to quality for 4-bit/8-bit quant?
03:28 Diego: quantization typically reduces memory and can allow higher packing on GPUs which drops cost, but there's a small quality delta depending on the model and task. For many retrieval-augmented short-answer tasks 4-bit is fine; for long-form generation you might prefer 8-bit or FP16. We can run side-by-side quality checks during the pilot.
03:45 Samir: so if we did Dedicated with reserved capacity, do you handle autoscaling for bursts or do we need burst credits?
03:51 Maya: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies and burst capacity. You can configure buffer lanes for bursts; there's also a hybrid routing option — keep a baseline dedicated pool and fall back to Hosted for spikes. That gives cost predictability plus resilience.
04:07 Lina: the fallback — is there any risk of data residency leak when falling back to Hosted? We need to ensure keys and PII don't leave our VPC.
04:15 Maya: good callout. For sensitive workloads Private or Dedicated with VPC peering and K M S integration avoids off-VPC routing. Fallback to Hosted can be configured to exclude sensitive routes; we can set routing policies so anything flagged as sensitive stays on your Dedicated/Private cluster.
04:31 Evan: we need SOC 2 and an audit log we can ship into our SIEM. Do you provide per-token tracing or just request-level logs?
04:38 Diego: we emit request-level traces and we can include token-level timing for performance debugging, but storing raw token text in logs is optional. For compliance we offer audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and K M S backed key encryption for Private. We'll share the security pack after the call.
04:55 Samir: what's Redwood's latency SLO on Dedicated for 7B-ish models?
05:00 Diego: for Dedicated with tuned batching we commonly hit 80–120ms median for short completions on modern GPUs for 7B-like models; tail depends on batching policy. If you need <200ms median you're in a comfortable zone. Hosted SLOs try to match but may have higher variance.
05:18 Evan: good. About benchmarking — we want a realistic test: 1k requests that mirror our mix (30% short 30–50 tokens, 70% ~220 tokens), run with and without caching. Can you run that?
05:28 Diego: yes we can. We'll model multiple batch sizes and continuous batching modes, and produce raw logs + per-token timing + cost estimate.
05:35 Maya: timeline for that would be about a week once we get sample prompts and a 1-2 hour window for cluster time — is that acceptable?
05:42 Lina: yes. We'll share prompts and the data shape. Another question — licensing and data retention: if we go Dedicated, do you retain any request payloads?
05:50 Maya: for Dedicated/Private you control log retention. By default we keep short-term operational logs for debugging, but we can disable persistent storage of request content if your compliance requires that.
06:01 Evan: competitors — we've talked with Anthropic and also using OpenAI for prototyping. Key differentiator for us is predictable unit economics and easy pilot-to-prod path.
06:11 Diego: understood. One more nuance: batching/caching interplay. If you have a lot of short queries, batching is less efficient, but you can use inference routing to favor cheaper model variants for short queries and reserve larger models for long-form tasks. That routing reduces unit costs without changing user experience in many cases.
06:33 Samir: are model variants something you maintain or do we bring our own models into Redwood Private?
06:38 Maya: both. We maintain a model catalog and curate quantized variants. For Private you can bring models and we support onboarding with our runtime; some kernel/compilation work is done during onboarding.
06:48 Lina: okay cost transparency — we need token-level cost reports for finance. Do you provide per-route token breakouts?
06:55 Diego: yes per-route and per-token cost breakdowns with traces. The console lets you slice by model, route, and token class. We'll give demo access in the pilot.
07:05 Evan: timeline: we're aiming to present to the execs in three weeks. So if we can get pilot numbers next week and a short runbook for expected monthly burn by 2028-03-06 that would be ideal.
07:16 Maya: that aligns: we'll send pricing spreadsheet Monday, run benchmark and share results by 2028-02-21, and then a compact ROI slide for exec review by 2028-02-24.
07:26 Lina: trust but verify — on quality, we need the model to match our in-house 7B baseline for intent classification; if quantized variant drops below 95% F1 we can't use it. Can you include classification evals in the benchmark?
07:36 Diego: absolutely. Please include the labeled eval set or a sampling. We'll run classification evals across variants and include delta metrics.
07:44 Evan: one more nit — our procurement requires a data processing addendum and an enterprise contract. Who handles that?
07:50 Maya: our sales ops and legal team will send the DPA and a standard enterprise term sheet; we can start NDAs and include the SOC 2 attestation. I'll loop in ops after this call.
07:59 Samir: bumping back to throughput — if Dedicated reduces cost but requires 3-month minimum reserve, how does the math move? Can you outline a simple compare?
08:08 Diego: sure, simple example: Dedicated reserved GPU amortized over expected throughput can lower per-token compute cost by 20–40% vs hosted, depending on utilization. But you must factor committed spend. We'll create a sensitivity table in the pricing sheet showing break-even utilization.
08:23 Evan: that sensitivity table is exactly what we need. Also include the hybrid fallback cost impact if we allow 20% of traffic to hit Hosted during spikes.
08:31 Maya: will do. Anything else on compliance or residency?
08:35 Lina: K M S integration — we need to rotate keys monthly and have HSM-backed keys. Is that supported?
08:41 Diego: yes for Private & Dedicated with K M S integration we support customer-managed keys and HSM-backed stores via partner K M S. We'll document the rotation and key lifecycle.
08:52 Evan: perfect. Okay recap?
08:54 Maya: recap — action items: 1) Maya share pilot pricing + sensitivity table and hosting comparison by 2028-02-16; 2) Diego run 1k request benchmark with their prompt mix, caching on/off, multiple batching profiles, include classification evals, deliver by 2028-02-21; 3) Crowne (Evan) share compliance contact and sample data shape by 2028-02-20 so we can configure Private/Dedicated onboarding. We'll also share security pack and SOC 2.
09:21 Lina: that works. We'll also confirm exec review date and follow up.
09:26 Maya: great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the pilot template and a short checklist.
09:32 Evan: thanks all.
